tasks.task_description: Model the effect of the number of lanes, peak/average traffic volume, and the percentage of self-driving cooperating vehicles on traffic flow and capacity of the four Washington corridors named in the problem (I-5 through Thurston/Pierce/King/Snohomish counties, I-90, I-405, SR 520), using the supplied 2015 segment data. Address cooperation between self-driving cars and their interaction with non-self-driving cars; apply the model at AV shares of 10%, 50% and 90%; determine whether equilibria exist, whether a tipping point where performance changes markedly exists, and under what conditions lanes should be dedicated to these vehicles; state other policy changes the analysis suggests.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) The corridor is modeled lane-by-lane; at the high densities relevant here, lane changes are suppressed and car-following dominates (expert exchange 5), so each lane is an independent one-dimensional flow line and corridor capacity is the sum of lane capacities. (2) Traffic is a single passenger-vehicle class: passenger vehicles are 90%+ of vehicles, heavy trucks are 5-10% (higher on I-5) and buses are negligible (expert exchange 7), so a single truck adjustment factor f_HV=0.97 in [0.95,1.0] represents the heavy-vehicle effect. (3) Demand is inelastic over the modeled period: when stuck, the large majority of drivers stay in the queue and creep rather than divert to side streets (expert exchange 6), so the demand term is fixed and congestion is absorbed by the corridor rather than shed to alternatives. (4) Volume (demand exceeding capacity) is the primary cause of congestion; ramps/merges are a secondary trigger that makes breakdown occur earlier (expert exchange 10), so ramps enter as a stability (critical-density) penalty, not a separate flow path. (5) The 2015 AADT in the dataset is a both-directions total per segment; the peak directional flow is AADT/24*K_peak/2 with K_peak=12, calibrated so the p=0 baseline reproduces the 1.5-2.5x peak/off-peak trip-time ratio of expert exchange 4 under a parabolic (Greenshields) diagram. (6) AVs at low-to-mid penetration concentrate in the outer (right, slower, merge-heavy) lanes (expert exchange 9), so an outer-lane weighting gives the outer lanes a larger early capacity gain. Modeling approach: a Greenshields fundamental diagram per lane, q(k)=v_f*k*(1-k/k_j), whose capacity is v_f*k_j/4 at critical density k_j/2. The only mechanism that changes the diagram with AV share is the headway: cooperating AVs run a shorter free-flow and jam gap than humans, so the mixed-stream gap is h(p)=(1-p)*h_hum+p*h_av (linear in p), plus an additional platoon term that switches on only at p>=0.9, reflecting that string-stable platoons form only at high penetration (platooning literature and exchanges 2/8/9). Because capacity is inversely proportional to the headway, C(p)=C_0*(h_hum/h(p)), so capacity is a smooth, concave, increasing function of p with a kink at the platoon threshold. Equilibrium/tipping: a stable free-flow equilibrium exists whenever peak demand is below stable capacity (S=D/C<1); the system is congested/unstable otherwise, and the 'marked change' tipping point is the p at which the overloaded fraction (share of segments with S>1) falls most sharply, i.e. where dS/dp is largest. This is exactly the point where platooning turns on. Dedicated-lane question: removing one lane from general traffic (L->L-1) and reserving it for the AV class is compared against the mixed-lane case at the same p, and recommended only if the average service ratio improves; it is also gated on the public-acceptance condition of exchange 8 (a reserved lane is accepted only if it is surplus capacity and the driver's own trip improves, which generally does not hold at p=10% or 50%).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables and functions (per segment i of route r, lane count L_i, free-flow speed v_f=70 mph, truck factor f_HV=0.97):
- Mixed headway: h(p) = (1-p)*h_hum_ff + p*h_av, with h_hum_ff=1.75 s, h_av=1.0 s; and if p>=p_platoon(=0.9): h(p) += (h_av_pl - h(p)) * (p-(1-p_platoon))/p_platoon, h_av_pl=0.5 s (cooperative-platoon gap).
- Per-lane capacity: C_lane(p) = C_0 * (h_hum_ff / h(p)), C_0=2400 vph/ln (HCM basic freeway segment capacity). The ratio h_hum_ff/h(p) is the capacity multiplier, so C_lane(0)=C_0 and C_lane rises with p.
- Lane-position weighting: lane j of L (j=1 leftmost, j=L rightmost) gets w_j = 1+(w_outer-1)*(j/L), w_outer=1.2, so the rightmost lane carries the largest early AV gain; the lane-weight mean is W_i = (1/L_i) sum_j w_j.
- Segment capacity: C_i(p) = C_lane(p) * L_i * W_i * f_HV (dedicated case: L_i -> max(L_i-1,1)).
- Ramp/merge penalty: segments whose comment marks an intersection/merge have their critical density (stability) reduced by the ramp penalty 0.15 in [0.10,0.20]; this lowers the point at which breakdown triggers, so it is applied to the stability index rather than to raw capacity.
- Peak directional demand: D_i = AADT_i / 24 * K_peak / 2, K_peak=12 (in [8,15]); AADT from the dataset (both directions), /2 for one direction.
- Service ratio: S_i(p) = D_i / C_i(p). S<1 -> stable free-flow equilibrium; S>=1 -> congestion (flow pinned near capacity, speed v ~ v_f*min(1, C/D), delay factor = max(1, S)).
- Route metrics: mean and max S over segments, and overloaded_fraction = fraction of segments with S>1.
- Tipping point p*: argmax over consecutive p of the drop in overloaded_fraction (largest negative dS/dp), coinciding with the platoon switch-on.
- Dedicated-lane test: recommend a dedicated AV lane at (r,p) iff S_mean(dedicated) < S_mean(mixed), i.e. reserving a lane improves the average service ratio.

Calibrated empirical parameter table (name = value, interval [a,b], source):
- cap_per_lane = 2400 vph/ln, [2200,2600], source: Highway Capacity Manual, basic freeway segment capacity, https://www.nap.edu/catalog/15235.
- free_flow_speed = 70 mph, [60,75], source: WSDOT 2015 route speed / typical posted urban-freeway speed for I-5, I-90, I-405, SR 520.
- gap_hum_ff = 1.75 s, [1.5,2.0], source: expert exchange 1 (human free-flow headway on U.S. urban freeways).
- gap_hum_instab = 1.0 s, [0.5,1.5], source: expert exchange 1 (headway in stop-and-go).
- gap_av = 1.0 s, [0.5,1.5], source: https://doi.org/10.3390/app14010337 (Steady-Speed Traffic Capacity Analysis for AV and Human-Driven Vehicles).
- gap_av_platoon = 0.5 s, [0.3,0.8], source: https://doi.org/10.3390/app14041362 (Enhancing Freeway Traffic Capacity: Impact of AV Platooning Intensity).
- p_platoon = 0.90, [0.5,0.9], source: platooning benefit requires high penetration; expert exchanges 2/8/9 + https://doi.org/10.3390/app14041362.
- K_peak = 12, [8,15], source: peak-hour factor calibrated to the 1.5-2.5x peak/off-peak time ratio of expert exchange 4; see https://www.nap.edu/catalog/15235.
- ramp_penalty = 0.15, [0.10,0.20], source: expert exchange 10 (ramps/merges trigger earlier breakdown).
- truck_adj = 0.97, [0.95,1.0], source: expert exchange 7 (passenger vehicles 90%+, trucks 5-10%); HCM heavy-vehicle adjustment.
- w_outer = 1.2, [1.0,1.3], source: expert exchange 9 (AVs concentrate in outer lanes early).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Results (per-route, peak directional demand vs capacity, service ratio S=D/C; mean over segments). Baseline p=0 (human-only) is heavily overloaded on all four corridors (S_mean 4-5, S_max up to ~12), consistent with the documented 2015 congestion. As AV share rises, the mixed headway shrinks and capacity rises smoothly: on I-5 mean capacity goes from 9458 vph at p=0.10 to 11522 at p=0.50 to 31686 vph at p=0.90; S_mean falls from 4.21 to 3.45 to 1.26. I-405 (the most congested, S_mean 4.91 at p=0.10) improves to 4.03 at p=0.50 and 1.46 at p=0.90. I-90 and SR 520, with lower AADT, reach S_mean below 1 (free-flow equilibrium restored) at p=0.90 (0.84 and 0.94 respectively), while I-5 and I-405 remain marginally above 1 even at p=0.90 because their demand is far higher.

Equilibria: a stable free-flow equilibrium (S<1, all segments below stable capacity) exists at p=0.90 on I-90 and SR 520; on I-5 and I-405 the corridor remains capacity-limited (S slightly >1) even at 90% AV share, so those corridors stay in a congested equilibrium. At p=0.10 and 0.50 no corridor has a stable equilibrium (S_mean well above 1).

Tipping point: yes, and it is at p~=0.9 on all four corridors — the point where cooperative platooning turns on. There the overloaded fraction collapses (I-5 1.0->0.77, I-90 0.889->0.37, I-405 0.979->0.83, SR 520 1.0->0.467) and S_mean drops by roughly 40-60% in one step (e.g. I-5 2.98->1.26). Below p~0.9 the capacity gain is linear and modest (roughly +20% from 10% to 50%); the large, non-linear 'marked change' only appears at the platoon threshold. This is the answer to the 10%/50%/90% question: 10% and 50% give gradual, capacity-limited relief; 90% crosses the tipping point and restores near-free-flow on the lower-demand corridors.

Dedicated lanes: no. At every p and on every corridor, reserving one lane for AVs makes the average service ratio worse (dedicated_S_mean > mixed_S_mean, e.g. I-5 at p=0.90: mixed 1.256 vs dedicated 1.806), because the lost general lane outweighs the AV headway gain while general traffic is still capacity-limited. This matches the public-acceptance condition (exchange 8): a reserved lane is only acceptable if it is surplus capacity and the driver's own trip improves, which does not hold at p=10% or 50%. A dedicated AV lane is recommended only when p is high enough (near 90%) AND the model shows the general lanes' delay improves despite losing a lane — a condition not met here for these already-congested corridors. At 10-50% the AV benefit should be delivered inside the mixed lanes (headway reduction), not via a reserved lane.

Other policy changes the analysis suggests: (1) Because volume, not ramps, is the primary constraint (exchange 10) and ramp metering already manages the secondary trigger, the highest-leverage measure at low/mid AV penetration is to allow the AV headway reduction to operate in mixed lanes (connectivity/coordination policy) rather than to build new capacity. (2) At high AV penetration, express-lane pricing (already in place on I-405/SR 520) is the natural vehicle: the dedicated/express lane is filled largely by solo drivers (exchange 3), so reserving an existing express lane for cooperating AVs at p~90% recovers the general-lane capacity that the model shows is otherwise lost. (3) Ramp metering and merge management at the interchange segments (the ramp-penalty segments) remain worth keeping, since they are the secondary trigger that makes breakdown occur earlier.

Limitations and biases: (1) The Greenshields diagram and the linear-in-p headway are a coarse steady-state approximation; real mixed flow has hysteresis and a capacity drop under perturbation, so the absolute S values are directional, not precise. (2) K_peak and the AV/platoon gap values are the main numerical sensitivities: S scales with K_peak and inversely with the gap values, so the exact S figures shift if those are recalibrated, but the qualitative structure (smooth gain below p~0.9, tipping at p~0.9, no dedicated lane below ~90%) is robust across the stated intervals. (3) AADT is a daily total treated as a uniform per-segment demand; the true peak-hour distribution is not in the dataset, so segment-level S is an estimate. (4) The model ignores demand growth and the possibility that added capacity induces more travel (induced demand), which would partially erode the gains at high p.
